en: The Śikṣā consisting of Verses on Vedic Terminology (Vedaparibhāṣākārikāśikṣā).
Now begins the Śikṣā consisting of Verses on Vedic Terminology.
[Salutations to] Śrī Rāma, the true Guru, Yājñavalkya, and likewise Kātyāyana.
Having paid homage, I shall state the definition of words consisting of four syllables.
In every section (*anuvāka*) of the Mādhyandina recension, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is proclaimed: a vowel, whether accompanied by consonants or alone, constitutes a syllable (*akṣara*).
The number of words is indicated by the first [mark]; by the second, the *visarga* and *nau*;

by the third, that which has an *avagraha* and that which has an *itikāra*; and by the fourth, that which ends in *m*, that which ends in a *kvādi* suffix, that which ends in a consonant (*hal*), and that which ends in *si* or *tu*, as well as that which has a *visarga*.
But that which is of a single form is uneven; in its absence, it is even or not [even].
4. The consonants from *ka* to *ha* are traditionally remembered as thirty-three;
however, the completion of the number is not by means of one [consonant], so one should effect a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) there. 5.
Excluding *ṛ* and *ḷ*, the vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *au* are ten;
however, in the first [group] and the second and subsequent groups, there are only nine, excluding *ā*. But when the letter *r* is placed above, there are ten or twenty.

In the nineteen [syllables] following the anusvāra, the lunar days (tithis) are recorded as seven. When multiplied by ten and increased by six, the number of words is obtained; in the first syllable, there are three consonants starting from the second, and the visarga and avagraha are represented by "ma."
The visarga situated in the middle of a word, at the end of a verse-quarter (padya), and at the end of a word;

likewise, the consonants *ka*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ṅa*, *ṇa*, *na*, *ma*, and the semivowels (*hala*) when they occur at the end of a verse-quarter or at the end of a word—these are the "white" (*sita*) syllables. (9–10)
This *Kārikā*, which comprises four verses, has been determined as a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) that facilitates the recitation and understanding of words;
thus ends the work composed by Paṇḍita Rāmacandra, son of the illustrious Paṇḍita Siddheśvara.
